frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, market viability, and ACR’s ability to capture value.
Any recommendation must be grounded in observable data, not assumptions or later developments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., personal distress beacon for outdoor enthusiasts) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into consumer market without differentiation (e.g., sell existing beacons directly to individual buyers).
3) No expansion – continue focusing on B2B/military/marine customers.
4) Pursue a different route to market (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers) or target a different customer segment (e.g., emergency preparedness kits for households).

T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers through outdoor retailers, bypassing traditional B2B channels, and capture premium prices for a differentiated product.

Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a reliable distress beacon.
Outdoor retailers are interested in stocking a new safety product.
predictions: Sales of 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in regions with high outdoor recreation activity.

Consumer price sensitivity will be moderate, allowing premium pricing for a differentiated model.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €250. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your household?" (binary yes/no). The test measures purchase intent for each segment.
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each segment

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and for household emergency preparedness buyers is <20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If the reverse is true, conclude T2 is better supported. If both segments show <20% intent, conclude neither theory is supported.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts’ intent ≥40% and household intent <20%, proceed with a limited pilot to test a differentiated model. If the test shows the reverse, or both segments’ “
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits)
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that is easy to use, reliable, and marketed as a safety tool for remote environments, sold directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or home‑improvement channels.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, collect data on purchase intent for each segment, and analyze results against the decision rule.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, or actual purchase behavior for outdoor enthusiasts or household emergency preparedness buyers.
would_change_if: If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts’ intent ≥40% and household intent <20%, the favoured theory would shift to T1 and the recommendation would be to proceed with a limited pilot.
If the test shows household intent ≥40% and outdoor intent <20%, the favoured theory would shift to T2 and the recommendation would be to explore a household‑focused proposition.
If both segments show <20% intent, neither theory would be supported and the recommendation would be to maintain the current B2B/military focus.

Any recommendation must be grounded in observable data, not assumptions or later developments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., personal distress beacon for outdoor enthusiasts) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into consumer market without differentiation (e.g., sell existing beacons directly to individual buyers).
3) No expansion – continue focusing on B2B/military/marine customers.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €250. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your household?" (binary yes/no). The test measures purchase intent for each segment.
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each segment

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and for household emergency preparedness buyers is <20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If the reverse is true, conclude T2 is better supported. If both segments show <20% intent, conclude neither theory is supported.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or market viability for 406 MHz distress beacons. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts outdoor enthusiasts will adopt the device because it provides a reliable emergency communication tool for remote environments. The theory remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts’ intent ≥40% and household intent <20%, proceed with a limited pilot to test a differentiated model. If the test shows the reverse, or both segments’ “
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits)
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides a reliable, easy-to-use emergency communication tool for remote environments, sold directly to consumers through outdoor retailers, with a premium price justified by differentiation.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, collect 200 responses, and analyze purchase intent by segment.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand, purchase intent, or market viability for 406 MHz distress beacons in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows household intent ≥40% and outdoor intent <20%, T2 would become the favoured theory and the recommendation would shift to targeting household emergency preparedness buyers.
If both segments show <20% intent, neither theory would be supported and the recommendation would remain unchanged.

arguments.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €250. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your household?" (binary yes/no). The test measures purchase intent for each segment.
arguments.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each segment

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and for household emergency preparedness buyers is <20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If the reverse is true, conclude T2 is better supported. If both segments show <20% intent, conclude neither theory is supported.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. arguments.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides a reliable, easy-to-use emergency communication tool for remote environments, sold directly to consumers through outdoor retailers, with a premium price justified by differentiation.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, collect 200 responses, and analyze purchase intent by segment.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, market viability, and ACR’s ability to capture value.
Any recommendation must be grounded in observable data, not assumptions or later developments.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., personal distress beacon for outdoor enthusiasts) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand into consumer market without differentiation (e.g., sell existing beacons directly to individual buyers).
3) No expansion – continue focusing on B2B/military/marine customers.
4) Pursue a different route to market (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers) or target a different customer segment (e.g., emergency preparedness kits for households).

T1.claim: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, easy-to-use emergency communication tool for remote environments, and ACR can capture value by selling directly to consumers through outdoor retailers.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) gain a safety device that can summon help in emergencies; ACR gains new revenue streams and brand exposure in consumer markets.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing outdoor recreation participation and awareness of remote-area safety needs create demand for a device that can be used independently of other communication methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers through outdoor retailers, bypassing traditional B2B channels, and capture premium prices for a differentiated product.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation in the U.S. is increasing.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a reliable distress beacon.
Outdoor retailers are interested in stocking a new safety product.
predictions: Sales of 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in regions with high outdoor recreation activity.
Retailers will allocate shelf space to the product if it demonstrates safety effectiveness.
Consumer price sensitivity will be moderate, allowing premium pricing for a differentiated model.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable, easy-to-use emergency communication tool for remote environments, and ACR can capture value by selling directly to consumers through outdoor retailers.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness households will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable backup communication tool for remote emergencies, and ACR can capture value by selling directly to consumers through home‑improvement retailers.
T2.who_benefits: Households gain a safety device that can be used in power outages or remote situations; ACR gains new revenue streams and brand exposure in consumer markets.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of emergency preparedness and the need for backup communication tools create demand for a device that can be used independently of other communication methods.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell directly to consumers through home‑improvement retailers, bypassing traditional B2B channels, and capture premium prices for a differentiated product.
assumptions: Household emergency preparedness spending is increasing.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a reliable backup communication device.
Home‑improvement retailers are interested in stocking safety products for emergency preparedness.
predictions: Sales of 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in regions with high household emergency preparedness activity.
Retailers will allocate shelf space to the product if it demonstrates safety effectiveness.
Consumer price sensitivity will be moderate, allowing premium pricing for a differentiated model.
T2.first_claim: Emergency preparedness households will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable backup communication tool for remote emergencies, and ACR can capture value by selling directly to consumers through home‑improvement retailers.

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €250. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your household?" (binary yes/no). The test measures purchase intent for each segment.
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 outdoor enthusiasts, 100 household emergency preparedness buyers)
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each segment

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and for household emergency preparedness buyers is <20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If the reverse is true, conclude T2 is better supported. If both segments show <20% intent, conclude neither theory is supported.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or market viability for 406 MHz distress beacons. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts outdoor enthusiasts will adopt the device because it provides a reliable emergency communication tool for remote environments. The theory remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure actual purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts versus household emergency preparedness buyers. If the test shows outdoor enthusiasts’ intent ≥40% and household intent <20%, proceed with a limited pilot to test a differentiated model. If the test shows the reverse, or both segments’ “
final.target_customer: Outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits)
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon that provides a reliable, easy-to-use emergency communication tool for remote environments, sold directly to consumers through outdoor retailers, with a premium price justified by differentiation.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, collect 200 responses, and analyze purchase intent by segment.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand, purchase intent, or market viability for 406 MHz distress beacons in 2002. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows household intent ≥40% and outdoor intent <20%, T2 would become the favoured theory and the recommendation would shift to targeting household emergency preparedness buyers.
If both segments show <20% intent, neither theory would be supported and the recommendation would remain unchanged.

arguments.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test for Outdoor Enthusiasts vs Household Emergency Preparedness
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, campers, climbers) and 100 household emergency preparedness buyers (households with emergency kits). Each respondent is shown a description of the 406 MHz distress beacon (same as in sources) and a price of €250. They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for yourself/your household?" (binary yes/no). The test measures purchase intent for each segment.

arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary yes/no) for each segment

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Household emergency preparedness buyers will show purchase intent of at least 40% (40 or more yes responses). Outdoor enthusiasts will show purchase intent of less than 20% (20 or fewer yes responses).

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for outdoor enthusiasts is ≥40% and for household emergency preparedness buyers is <20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If the reverse is true, conclude T2 is better supported. If both segments show <20% intent, conclude neither theory is supported.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey (X1) to test demand for a premium model versus demand for durability/reliability. If the survey shows a purchase rate ≥50% and average willingness to pay ≥$500, proceed to develop a premium model; otherwise, focus on existing dealer network and existing product lines.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, and identify the key evidence that would support this decision.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; cannot use later developments.
No internal company data; must rely on external evidence.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
Must consider the existing dealer network and individual buyer reach of Deere.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, residential lawn care, or a niche industrial application).
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the existing tractor, combine, and industrial equipment markets through dealers.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products (if feasible).

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work, and Deere can capture value by offering a high‑quality product through its existing dealer network.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers who need a functional, long‑lasting tractor for lawn and garden tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: These consumers currently rely on generic lawn mowers or other brands; they will switch to Deere if they perceive Deere as a trusted, durable brand that is readily available through existing dealers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors directly to dealers, who then sell to consumers, earning a margin on each unit and building brand loyalty that can support future sales.
assumptions: Deere’s existing dealer network can reach individual buyers effectively.
Consumers value durability and reliability over price.
Deere can produce tractors at a cost that allows a dealer margin.

X1.method: Online survey of 200 individual homeowners and small‑holder farmers in the United States, recruited via a panel. Participants are asked about their current lawn and garden equipment (brand, model, age), their willingness to pay for a premium lawn and garden tractor, and their interest in a differentiated consumer proposition from Deere (e.g., a model with enhanced comfort, ease of use, or additional features). The survey also asks about their primary purchase criteria (e.g., durability, price, brand trust).
X1.sample: 200 participants, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to reflect the target market.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: binary choice between "Would purchase a differentiated Deere consumer lawn and garden tractor" (Yes/No). Secondary outcomes: (a) average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for a premium model; (b) perceived importance of comfort/ease of use (1‑5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will choose "Would purchase" at a rate ≥ 50% because they need a reliable, durable machine for routine yard work and trust Deere’s brand through dealers.

X1.name: Deere Premium vs. Standard Consumer Survey
X1.method: Online survey with 500 respondents recruited from households with small gardens (under 1 acre) in the United States. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a description of a standard Deere lawn and garden tractor (base model, no premium features) with a price of $1,500. Group B sees the same tractor described as a premium model (same base features but with additional styling, brand prestige messaging, and a price of $2,000). Both groups are asked the same questions about willingness to pay, perceived quality, and brand trust. The survey also collects demographic data (age, household income, and prior lawn and garden tractor ownership).
X1.sample: 500 respondents, recruited via an online panel to match the target demographic of small‑holder gardeners.
X1.measure: 1) Primary outcome: average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for each tractor description. 2) Secondary outcomes: perceived quality score (1‑10), brand trust score (1‑10), and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A (standard model) will have a higher average WTP than Group B (premium model) because consumers value durability and reliability over price premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B (premium model) will have a higher average WTP than Group A because consumers are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige and superior user experience.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group B exceeds Group A by at least $200 (a 15% premium), we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than $200, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the difference is $200 or more in favor of Group A, we cannot distinguish between the theories and conclude both are plausible.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey test (X1) to empirically compare willingness to pay for a standard model versus a premium model. The test will determine whether consumers value durability and reliability over price premium, which would support T1, or whether they are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige, which would support T2. arguments.name: Deere Premium vs. Standard Consumer Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with 500 respondents recruited from households with small gardens (under 1 acre) in the United States. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a description of a standard Deere lawn and garden tractor (base model, no premium features) with a price of $1,500. Group B sees the same tractor described as a premium model (same base features but with additional styling, brand prestige messaging, and a price of $2,000). Both groups are asked the same questions about willingness to pay, perceived quality, and brand trust. The survey also collects demographic data (age, household income, and prior lawn and garden tractor ownership).
arguments.sample: 500 respondents, recruited via an online panel to match the target demographic of small‑holder gardeners.
arguments.measure: 1) Primary outcome: average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars for each tractor description. 2) Secondary outcomes: perceived quality score (1‑10), brand trust score (1‑10), and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A (standard model) will have a higher average WTP than Group B (premium model) because consumers value durability and reliability over price premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B (premium model) will have a higher average WTP than Group A because consumers are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige and superior user experience.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average WTP for Group B exceeds Group A by at least $200 (a 15% premium), we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than $200, we conclude T1 is better supported. If the difference is $200 or more in favor of Group A, we cannot distinguish between the theories and conclude both are plausible.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with randomized presentation of two lawn tractor concepts: a basic, low‑price model emphasizing affordability and practicality, and a premium model emphasizing status and skill. Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the United States. They are shown a brief description of the tractor, its price range, and a statement about its intended use (e.g., "perfect for small‑hold lawn care and easy to use for various chores"). They are then asked to indicate their primary motivation for purchasing a lawn tractor (price, practicality, status, or skill).
X1.sample: 500 households with small gardens (under 1 acre) in the United States, recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Primary motivation selected by participants (price, practicality, status, or skill). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for each tractor concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select "price" or "practicality" as their primary motivation, and the average WTP for the basic model will be at least $600.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select "status" or "skill" as their primary motivation, and the average WTP for the premium model will be at least $1,200.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants selecting "price" or "practicality" is ≥60% and the average WTP for the basic model is ≥$600, T1 is supported. If the proportion selecting "status" or "skill" is ≥60% and the average WTP for the premium model is ≥$1,200, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions: one emphasizing affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance (T1), and one emphasizing status, prestige, and community signaling (T2). Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the U.S. and asked to indicate their primary reason for purchasing a lawn and garden tractor (e.g., "affordability and practicality" vs. "status and prestige").
X1.sample: 500 households with small gardens (defined as less than 1 acre) in the U.S., recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Primary reason for purchase: (a) affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance; (b) status, prestige, and community signaling.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance as their primary reason for purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select status, prestige, and community signaling as their primary reason for purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants selecting affordability/practicality is at least 10 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting status/prestige, T1 is supported. If status/prestige is at least 10 percentage points higher, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, the evidence is inconclusive.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions: one emphasizing affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance (T1), and one emphasizing status, prestige, and community signaling (T2). Participants are recruited from households with small gardens in the U.S. and asked to indicate their primary reason for purchasing a lawn and garden tractor (e.g., "affordability and practicality" vs. "status and prestige").
arguments.sample: 500 households with small gardens (defined as less than 1 acre) in the U.S., recruited via an online panel to ensure geographic diversity.
arguments.measure: Primary reason for purchase: (a) affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance; (b) status, prestige, and community signaling.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of participants will select affordability, practicality, and ease of maintenance as their primary reason for purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of participants will select status, prestige, and community signaling as their primary reason for purchase.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of participants selecting affordability/practicality is at least 10 percentage points higher than the proportion selecting status/prestige, T1 is supported. If status/prestige is at least 10 percentage points higher, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, the evidence is inconclusive.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

X1.name: Small‑holder vs Status‑driven Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Recruit 200 respondents: 100 self‑identified small‑holder farmers (defined as owning at least one tractor for farming) and 100 homeowners (defined as owning a home but not a tractor). Randomly assign each respondent to one of two scenarios: (A) a basic lawn‑and‑garden tractor priced at $1,500; (B) a premium‑priced version of the same tractor priced at $2,500, marketed as a status‑symbol and brand‑ prestige product. In each scenario, ask: "Would you purchase this tractor?" (binary yes/no) and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open‑ended).
X1.sample: 200 respondents (100 small‑holders, 100 homeowners)
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Small‑holder farmers will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price willingness than homeowners, because they already own tractors and need a single machine for both farm and garden tasks.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and higher maximum price willingness than small‑holders, because they value brand prestige and status, and are willing to pay a premium for a premium brand.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for homeowners is at least 10 percentage points higher than for small‑holders, conclude that T2 is better supported. If the average maximum price willingness for homeowners is at least $500 higher than for small‑holders, conclude that T2 is better supported. If neither condition is met, conclude that neither theory is strongly supported.

final.next_action: Run the Small‑holder vs Status‑driven Purchase Intent Test to measure purchase intent and price willingness between small‑holders and homeowners.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence from 1962 about small‑holder farmers’ demand or homeowners’ status‑driven purchasing behavior. The test is needed to resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowners are at least 10 percentage points more likely to purchase and willing to pay at least $500 more, the favoured theory would shift to T2.
If the test shows no significant difference between small‑holders and homeowners, both theories would be weakened and a different approach would be considered.
